lines: Trigger the exact same checkpoint, on the exact same backed-up input, under two different settings.
One of those settings takes forever to finish. The other barely notices the backlog is even there.
Same backlog, same job, same moment. The only thing that changed is which mode was chosen.
Running continuously doesn't mean nothing ever breaks. A single worker can still fail, mid job, without warning.
Recovering from that cleanly means having a consistent picture of every bit of state, taken while things keep moving.
Getting that picture, without ever pausing the whole job to take it, is the actual problem here.
One small signal gets sent in alongside the ordinary data, flowing through exactly the same paths everything else does.
Once every path into a given step has carried that signal, that step has seen everything from before it clean.
That's an old idea from distributed snapshots, borrowed almost whole, just carried by the data itself this time.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
One path into a step is badly clogged with work nobody's gotten to yet, right as that signal gets sent.
Does the signal just wait behind all that clogged-up work, or does it somehow skip past it instead?
answer: Depends entirely on which setting got chosen beforehand.
One setting makes the signal wait its turn behind everything clogged ahead of it, on every single path in.
The other setting acts the moment the signal shows up at all, clog and all, no waiting required.

lines: Pick the waiting setting, and a step holds off on doing anything until that signal has arrived everywhere at once.
One badly clogged path drags that arrival out, and everything else sits there waiting on it to catch up.
The whole snapshot only moves as fast as its single slowest path, every single time, by design.
Pick the other setting, and a step acts the instant it sees that signal on even just one path.
Whatever was still sitting there, clogged and unprocessed, just gets folded straight into the picture being taken.
Nothing waits. The picture just ends up carrying more inside it than it otherwise would have.
Taking a brand new full picture every single time gets more expensive the longer a job has been running.
Taking only what's changed since the last picture stays the same size, no matter how much came before it.
One grows without any limit at all. The other stays flat, bounded only by what just happened.
Worth reasoning through once more before this reveal settles it.
The stricter guarantee about what gets processed costs more to keep up, every single time it runs.
Is paying that extra cost still the right call to make by default, or does a cheaper option usually win?
answer: The stricter guarantee is still what gets chosen by default, for almost everything.
The cheaper option risks quietly processing the same piece of work twice after a failure, which matters for most jobs.
Only work that truly can't tolerate any extra waiting at all should ever reach for the cheaper one.

lines: Under the stricter guarantee, nothing gets double counted, ever, no matter how a failure happens to land.
Under the cheaper one, a failure can occasionally mean the same piece of work gets handled twice over.
Most work should take the stricter guarantee. Only the most latency-sensitive work should ever trade it away.
One kind of picture gets taken automatically, over and over, owned entirely by the system running the job.
A different kind of picture only ever gets taken on purpose, by someone who wants it, for a reason.
That second kind is built to survive a job changing shape on purpose, not just a plain failure.
Every number in this reel came from one real run, happening just now, of this topic's own toy model.
The waiting setting that really did wait. The other setting that really barely slowed down on the same backlog.
And the picture-taking cost that really did stay flat, even as the full version kept climbing on its own.
So: a signal that travels with the data itself, borrowed from an old idea about distributed snapshots.
Wait for it everywhere and pay for whatever's slowest, or act the moment it shows up and carry more along.
One picture gets taken automatically and owned by the system. A different picture only gets taken on purpose.
